title: HTTP
summary: The protocol almost all web backends are built on.
why: Every API an AI generates speaks HTTP. If you cannot tell an idempotent retry from a duplicate charge, you cannot tell whether the generated code is safe.

cards.question: What does it mean for an HTTP method to be idempotent?
cards.answer: Repeating the same request leaves the server in the same final state. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.

cards.question: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
cards.answer: 401: unauthenticated, valid credentials are missing. 403: the server knows who you are but you lack permission for that resource.

cards.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
cards.answer: PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH applies a partial change. PUT is idempotent by definition, PATCH depends on its implementation.

cards.question: How does conditional caching with ETag work?
cards.answer: The server sends an ETag identifying the version. The client resends it in If-None-Match; if unchanged, the server replies 304 with no body and the client reuses its copy.

cards.question: What is CORS and what is the preflight for?
cards.answer: A browser policy restricting cross-origin requests; the server declares allowed origins with Access-Control-Allow-Origin. For non-simple requests the browser first sends an OPTIONS (preflight) asking whether they are allowed. It does not protect the server, only the user in the browser.

cards.question: What problem does HTTP/2 solve compared to HTTP/1.1?
cards.answer: Stream multiplexing over a single TCP connection, removing HTTP-level head-of-line blocking, and header compression with HPACK. TCP-level blocking remains; HTTP/3 (QUIC) fixes it.
